raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the first clinically successful angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) for heart failure (HF). Its rationale is physiologic: natriuretic peptide signaling promotes natriuresis, vasodilatation, cyclic guanosine monophosphate generation, anti-fibrotic signaling, and suppression of renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic activation [1]. Sacubitril is converted to the neprilysin inhibitor LBQ657, while valsartan blocks angiotensin II type-1 receptors, avoiding the isolated-neprilysin problem of increased angiotensin II and the vasopeptidase-inhibitor problem of excessive bradykinin-mediated angioedema [2,3]. Because neprilysin inhibition increases BNP but not NT-proBNP, NT-proBNP is preferred for early biochemical assessment after initiation.

The pivotal HFrEF evidence is PARADIGM-HF, designed to test dual ARNI against proven-dose enalapril in symptomatic ambulatory patients after sequential run-in exposure to both drugs [4]. In 8442 randomized patients, sacubitril/valsartan reduced cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, and all-cause mortality versus enalapril, establishing ARNI as a disease-modifying replacement for ACE inhibition in eligible HFrEF patients [5]. Subsequent analyses showed that benefit extended beyond first events: sacubitril/valsartan slowed clinical progression, reduced intensification of HF therapy and emergency visits [6], reduced both sudden death and death from worsening HF [7], and retained relative efficacy across age groups [8], dose reductions [9], baseline systolic blood pressure strata [10], prior decompensation categories [11], and recurrent-event analyses [12]. Biomarker work in PARADIGM-HF linked early NT-proBNP reduction with improved prognosis and clarified BNP interpretation during neprilysin inhibition [13,14].

Implementation studies broadened the evidence from stable outpatients to hospitalized or recently decompensated HFrEF. TITRATION showed that initiation and up-titration were feasible with condensed or conservative schedules, particularly when starting dose was adjusted to previous renin–angiotensin system exposure and blood pressure [15]. PIONEER-HF randomized stabilized patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF and demonstrated greater NT-proBNP reduction with in-hospital sacubitril/valsartan than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [16]. Exploratory clinical and biomarker analyses suggested fewer early rehospitalization events and reductions in markers of myocardial injury and stress [17,18]. The open-label extension supported switching from enalapril to sacubitril/valsartan after discharge, while dose-level analyses suggested benefit even among patients not achieving target dose [19,20]. TRANSITION complemented these data by showing that pre-discharge and early post-discharge initiation were both feasible in stabilized patients [21,22].

Reverse remodeling is a plausible mediator of benefit. PROVE-HF associated NT-proBNP decline after sacubitril/valsartan initiation with improvements in left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, and atrial volume over 12 months [23]. EVALUATE-HF did not significantly improve its primary aortic-stiffness endpoint versus enalapril, but supported tolerability and suggested favorable effects on some echocardiographic filling-pressure measures [24]. These studies reinforce that ARNI should not be viewed simply as a vasodilator or diuretic-sparing agent, but as neurohormonal therapy with structural and biochemical effects.

In HFpEF and HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction, evidence is more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction with LCZ696 than valsartan in HFpEF and generated the phase 3 hypothesis [25]. Renal analyses in PARAMOUNT suggested slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate but more albuminuria [26]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death in LVEF ≥45%, although it suggested benefit for HF hospitalizations, women, and patients with LVEF below the normal range [27]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicate that sacubitril/valsartan benefit diminishes as LVEF rises, with the clearest signal in HFrEF and possible extension into HFmrEF or “lower-range” HFpEF [28,29].

Clinically, sacubitril/valsartan is now guideline-directed foundational therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF and is considered for selected patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF, especially when LVEF is toward the lower end of the preserved range [30]. Practical use requires a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors, avoidance in prior angioedema or pregnancy, and monitoring for hypotension, renal function, and potassium. Remaining questions include optimal sequencing with SGLT2 inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and beta-blockers; use in advanced kidney disease; and defining responders across sex, obesity, atrial fibrillation, and LVEF phenotypes. Overall, ARNI therapy has changed HF care by converting natriuretic peptide augmentation from a biologic concept into outcome-improving therapy.
